title: Ranking All 20 Premier League Teams’ Performances on Matchday 7
subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Grey Whitebloom6:30 PM EDTAlexander Isak (left) and Bruno Fernandes had very different weekends. / Marc Atkins/Getty Images (Isak), Mark Cosgrove/News Images/NurPhoto/Getty Images (Fernandes)This was a Premier League weekend of landmarks.

Chelsea kept their first top-flight clean sheet since January; Dejan Kulusevski played his first Tottenham Hotspur match in 526 days; Manchester United had their first “fresh start” since midweek and Enzo Maresca became the first manager to win his opening seven Premier League games at a new club—ever.

It remains to be seen what fragments of history are preserved once Manchester City’s ongoing battle with the Premier League is brought to a merciful conclusion. But amid this legal limbo, the action on the pitch is the only solid ground we have to stand on.

Sunderland are struggling to balance Europe and the Premier League. / Ryan Pierse/Getty ImagesKevin Danso’s 17th-minute red card can only partly be used as mitigation for this desperate implosion. Sunderland were already 1–0 down (thanks in part to a Danso blunder) and could have conceded another by the time the defender was dismissal. “If I have to be honest with you, we are not good,” the Black Cats fullback Nordi Mukiele damningly admitted. “Maybe because we became arrogant, maybe. This is what I think.”

This was a day for Pierre Sage to forget as swiftly as he can. / Sebastian Frej/Getty ImagesPierre Sage summed it up pretty succinctly: “My feeling after the game is shame.” It would have been a common sensation in the Crystal Palace locker room.

There were no goals for Hull City. / Jacques Feeney/Offside/Getty Images“It’s easy to analyze this game,” Hull City boss Sergej Jakirović quietly fumed. “We were out of everything.”The Tigers were dutifully outshot, outrun and out-thought by their under-pressure hosts. Fulham dominated every conceivable aspect of the contest, making a mockery of their 1–0 margin of victory. Jakirović offered a more telling reflection that the scoreline: “It was men against boys.”

This was not a fun one for those from Tyneside. / Stu Forster/Getty ImagesThis was an damning contrast of control and chaos for Newcastle United. While Aston Villa played with the collective calm of a team benefitting from a three-second radio delay, the Magpies were left to thrash around in real time, haphazardly haring about the place, never too near to goal. For a team that is so willfully gung-ho, and spent more than $225 million on forwards in less than two years, Newcastle were left to rely upon the 6'7" merchant of chaos, Dan Burn, as a late striker option.“We were not smart enough,” Matthias Jaissle curtly concluded.

Frank Lampard had an unfamiliar feeling in north London. / Marc Atkins/Getty ImagesDuring Frank Lampard’s playing days at Chelsea, Tottenham’s home ground was uncharitably known as “Three Point Lane” rather than White Hart Lane, such was the lopsided nature of the London rivalry at the time. Lampard’s Coventry City left the capital with zero points on Monday after failing to capitalize upon a strong start and fast finish to a night of rare euphoria for the hosts.

Harrison Armstrong (left) got his manager’s approval if not the referee’s. / Mike Morese/MI News/NurPhoto/Getty ImagesIt says everything that David Moyes hailed Harrison Armstrong’s crunching challenge on Josh Acheampong as “the best part” of the goalless first half.Considering the Toffees conceded two cheap goals while taking just two shots in a tame second 45 minutes, that tackle was probably the highlight of Moyes’s afternoon. And it was a foul.

Referee John Brooks decided the game. / Charlotte Wilson/Offside/Getty ImagesThis game swung violently on the tamest act that could conceivably be deemed as violent conduct. Yehor Yarmoliuk’s timid brush of his head toward Jérémy Jacquet warranted the red card which it received, although his battling teammates scarcely deserved the change in momentum they would be unable to control thereafter.
Zian's second goal for Town. 👊 pic.twitter.com/eRB81mBOQI

“The aim was to come here and cause them problems and get points,” Dara O’Shea reflected. Ipswich achieved half of that, bloodying Manchester City’s nose without coming too close to getting that knockout blow.
🎯 "DCL WITH A CLINICAL FINISH!" pic.twitter.com/ScKix8gXjO

It says plenty about where Leeds are at that Daniel Farke could come away from a draw with Manchester United and be justifiably disappointed with a point. Yet, this was not a case of wasted chances or bad luck. Leeds played the occasion rather than the opposition in the first half, timidly prodding at a United side very much there for the taking. As underwhelming as the visitors have been, even this iteration of the Red Devils can’t be given a 45-minute head start and still lose.
Back-to-back #PL goals for @BMbeumo19 ⚽️ pic.twitter.com/tWTDqIXc3i

The bright lights perennially beaming down upon Manchester United seem to be more blinding than most. A much-improved display against Atlético Madrid inspired Lisandro Martínez to give Jason Wilcox a public job review. A performance at Elland Road worthy of little more than a disinterested shrug somehow convinced Michael Carrick to hail a “fresh start.”There was a fresh tactical approach which spelled out United’s place in the current hierarchy. Carrick didn’t deploy a new formation so much as set his players with 11 individual tasks, each one predicated on what their Leeds counterparts were doing at that exact moment. This grand show of inferiority did not tighten a leaky rearguard or improve their porous press but it did at least get a point.
Noni delivers the defining moment 🎯 pic.twitter.com/c8o1UErdlJ

The James Bond villain Auric Goldfinger tells 007: “Once is happenstance. Twice is a coincidence. Three times is enemy action.” Arsenal were their own worst enemies for the third match in succession at the City Ground.Just as in the wins over Leeds and Lille, Mikel Arteta’s champions didn’t bother turning up for the opening hour. Just as in those narrow victories, the team’s substitutes inspired a win which didn’t offer an overwhelming amount of confidence.Arteta has publicly vaunted the positives of this sequence, namely Arsenal’s strength in depth and an ability to “manage the emotional part” of matches. Yet, if fans hope to endure any overriding emotions aside from frustration (followed by relief) it may be an idea to start brightly for once.

Liam Delap had no shortage of spurned chances. / Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty ImagesThis was an 80-minute masterpiece in how to play Arsenal from Nottingham Forest. Martin Ødegaard was put in a jail of red fabric, Bukayo Saka shunted to the fringes and Eberechi Eze bulldozed into a halftime withdrawal. Matz Sels didn’t even have to make a save. Unfortunately, Forest’s goalkeeper would end the game without denying Arsenal’s only shot on target, which was diverted by a cruel double deflection.The only criticism for Oliver Glasner’s side was a familiar one: no clinical composure. It’s now more than eight hours of soccer since Forest last scored a goal in front of their home fans.
